Eggs of the Trout-perch Percopsis omiscomaycus undergo development at a temperature of 21.5 °C [T = 21.5 °C], with the hatching event occurring after an incubation period of 6.5 days . The newly emerged prolarvae measure just 0.53 cm  in total length at hatch, a diminutive size that reflects the species’ relatively small egg diameter of approximately 1.87 mm. Following yolk-sac resorption and the transition to exogenous feeding, the age at birth—defined here as the point at which the yolk-sac larva becomes a free-swimming fry capable of independent foraging—is reached at 12.1 days [ab = 12.1 days] since fertilisation under the same thermal regime of 21.5 °C [T = 21.5 °C]. This rapid early development, completing the entire embryonic and yolk-sac larval phase in about 12 days total, is typical of small-bodied percopsiform fishes that exploit productive but seasonally constrained freshwater habitats. The wet weight at birth for these nascent fry is remarkably low at 0.0034 grams [Wwb = 0.0034 grams], a value derived from the spherical egg geometry and consistent with the minimal energy reserves that must sustain the larva through the critical window between hatching and first feeding.

As the juveniles grow, they undergo a sustained period of somatic expansion before reaching reproductive competence. Field surveys indicate that the total length at birth is approximately 0.8 cm [Lb = approximately 0.8 cm], representing the size of the free-swimming fry immediately after the completion of yolk absorption. From this modest starting point, individuals progress through a fingerling stage characterized by rapid linear growth. The onset of sexual maturation in females is closely tied to body size, with the total length at puberty recorded at 5.4 cm [Lp = 5.4 cm]. At this developmental milestone, the corresponding wet weight at puberty, calculated from a length–weight relationship typical of the species, reaches approximately 1.76 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.76 grams]. This threshold marks the point at which vitellogenesis and gonadal recrudescence are initiated, enabling females to participate in the upcoming spawning season. The transition from immature juvenile to a reproductively viable organism involves considerable energetic investment, as the individual must more than double its body length from the birth size to the puberty size while accumulating sufficient lipid reserves to support gamete production.

Reproductive output in Trout-perch has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions held at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], which approximates the thermal environment experienced during the spring spawning season in north-temperate lakes. At a reference body length of 14.6 cm—a size near the upper end of the adult size distribution—females produce approximately 1329 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 1329 eggs per year], corresponding to a reproductive rate at L 14.6 cm of approximately 3.64 eggs per day  at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This value translates into a substantial annual fecundity given the protracted spawning period characteristic of the species. It is worth noting that this rate is measured specifically at a body length of 14.6 cm, and individual variation around this mean is considerable, influenced by factors such as maternal condition, age, and local food availability. The high reproductive rate reflects an evolutionary strategy that compensates for elevated egg and larval mortality in the unpredictable environments these fish inhabit, where optimal spawning conditions may be brief and interannual variability in recruitment is pronounced.

The ultimate total length attained by Trout-perch in most wild populations is 20 cm [Li = 20 cm], a size that represents the maximum recorded across the species’ range. Corresponding to this maximum length, the ultimate wet weight reaches approximately 90 grams [Wwi = approximately 90 grams], a value derived from the empirical length–weight scaling relationship. Males and females both approach this upper size limit, though females tend to be slightly larger on average, a dimorphism likely linked to the selective advantage of increased fecundity in larger individuals. At a more intermediate size, such as the 12.5 cm  length that corresponds to a body mass of 20.56 grams , individuals are already fully mature and actively contributing to the spawning population. This size is often sampled in gillnet surveys, and the associated mass provides a useful calibration point for fisheries biologists assessing the condition factor of local stocks. The growth trajectory from the 0.8 cm birth length to the 20 cm ultimate length involves an approximately 25-fold increase in linear dimensions.

Longevity and reproductive timing in Percopsis omiscomaycus are tightly coupled to the thermal conditions of their environment. Under a thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], which typifies the average summer temperatures of the mesotrophic lakes this species frequents, the maximum lifespan is estimated at 730 days [am = 730 days], representing a two-year life cycle. At the same temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the first reproduction event—defined as the first successful spawning—occurs at approximately 730 days after hatching [tR = approximately 730 days after hatching] for females, aligning closely with the lifespan estimate and indicating a largely semelparous reproductive schedule in many populations. Males, however, may mature somewhat later, with some records suggesting an age at first reproduction of up to 6 years after hatching [tR = up to 6 years after hatching] under cooler conditions, though such extended lifespans are exceptional and likely confined to the northernmost portions of the species’ distribution. This compressed life history, with first reproduction occurring nearly at the end of the maximum lifespan, underscores the intense selective pressure on early growth and rapid maturation in a short-lived fish that must reproduce before senescence imposes physiological constraints.
